transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-11
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CTO - Blackwell), Sam Ortiz (Infra), Ellen Park (Security), Kenji Sato (DevOps), Rajiv Patel (ML)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery for a fully isolated, no-network enclave deployment. Customer is regulated diagnostics lab; high focus on offline image distribution, signed artifacts, key management (HSM), SOC2/ISO alignment, and hardware constraints (older GPUs, limited egress). Discussed latency expectations, upgrade/patch cadence and rollback strategy for no-network environment. Next steps: share checklist, hardware sizing, schedule benchmarks.

Topics: scope of isolation, update process for models & runtime, image signing & verification, licensing & activation without internet, monitoring & audit logs, fallback for model regressions, HW sizing and quantization strategy

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Maya (AE): Okay, good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 55 minutes, we'll keep this focused — Diego and I will run through our typical enclave/private deployment topics and then leave time for questions.

[00:00:24] Priya (CTO): Thanks, Maya. We wanted to get into the weeds because this will be deployed in our diagnostics lab network which is physically isolated — no outbound, no inbound, so we need a complete plan for images, updates and audits.

[00:00:39] Diego (SE): Right, perfect. To confirm, when you say physically isolated, do you mean no internet at all from the cluster? And are there any controlled jump boxes or an air-gapped transfer station?

[00:00:53] Sam (Infra): Correct — the compute cluster is on an internal VLAN with no routing to the internet. We have a controlled transfer node in a secure room where ops can bring USB or an encrypted HDD, that's the only mechanism for bringing artifacts in.

[00:01:09] Ellen (Security): And to add, anything brought in must be scanned and verified, checksummed, and approved by security. We also require hardware-based key storage — an HSM — and strict RBAC for who can trigger an update.

[00:01:24] Diego (SE): Understood. Two immediate things we think about: 1) signed container images / signed model artifacts, and 2) an offline activation/license flow so the runtime can validate entitlements without phoning home. We support a signed artifact workflow where you bring the image tarball and a detached signature, we verify SHA256 and signature against a Redwood public key that you hold.

[00:01:46] Priya (CTO): That sounds good; does Redwood provide the signing keys or do we manage them? We prefer to manage keys in our HSM.

[00:01:58] Maya (AE): We can do both. Standard option is Redwood signs artifacts and you import our public verification key into your trust store. For higher assurance customers, you can sign artifacts with your own key and we can verify with policy. We'll document both flows in the checklist.

[00:02:18] Rajiv (ML): On the model side — we're evaluating a 8B-13B family model for inference. Our GPU fleet is mixed; a couple of older T4s and one A5000, most workloads will be CPU-only unless we provision additional cards. How does Redwood handle quantized CPU execution vs GPU fallback?

[00:02:39] Diego (SE): Good question. Our private runtime can run on CPU with int8/4 quantized kernels; performance will obviously be slower than a GPU but for many diagnostic tasks throughput is bounded by p95 latency of small inputs. We can provide a recommend HW footprint — e.g., for 13B int8 on CPU expect X rps per core — and recommend a small GPU for tail latency if you need sub-200ms p95. We'll include bench numbers in the HW proposal.

[00:03:05] Kenji (DevOps): Important to note — power & cooling is constrained, we can't add racks easily. If the recommendation is to add GPUs we need a justification and a phased plan.

[00:03:18] Diego (SE): Totally — part of the POC is to run your sample requests (anonymized) on our bench to show delta between CPU quantized and a single A5000. If the cost/space doesn't justify GPUs, we can also explore smaller model family or more aggressive quantization and token-efficiency prompts.

[00:03:38] Priya (CTO): What about continuous rollout? We can't have nodes reach out to pull updates. How do you do safe rollouts and rollback without network access?

[00:03:51] Diego (SE): We do an artifactory-based approach for air-gapped sites. You prepare a signed bundle containing the runtime, model shards, and a deployment manifest. Ops transfers the bundle to the transfer node. The local orchestration verifies signatures, runs a dry-run verify and can perform a canary on a subset of nodes. Rollback is supported by keeping previous bundles on the local private registry. All orchestration happens locally — no outbound required.

[00:04:14] Ellen (Security): Who holds the private keys for the signing? If Redwood is signing, that means the private key is externally held. We prefer to sign ourselves with keys in our HSM and only accept customer-signed packages.

[00:04:26] Maya (AE): That's fine — customers signing their own packages is an established path. We'll include the verification step and policy definitions in the handoff doc.

[00:04:38] Priya (CTO): Auditability is non-negotiable. We need tamper-evident logs, local audit trails with immutability, and exportable proofs for regulators. How do you capture metrics and logs when the control plane is local?

[00:04:53] Diego (SE): The private control plane runs locally in your enclave. We provide a log collector that writes signed audit events to an append-only store. For extra assurance we can sign events with a local key in the HSM; logs are exportable as a bundle that you can ship to a compliance archive. There's also an offline metrics exporter we can configure to write deltas to a USB for external ingestion.

[00:05:16] Sam (Infra): Any remote observability? We do not want telemetry leaving the enclave but we do want to see local SLOs and error rates.

[00:05:26] Diego (SE): By default no telemetry leaves the enclave. The console can be installed on a jump host that has read-only access to the local API, or you can use our local web UI. If you later choose to enable secure integration with Redwood hosted console, that's optional and requires explicit authorization and pinned circuits.

[00:05:41] Priya (CTO): License activation — we want offline activation tied to a hardware fingerprint or HSM. Is that supported?

[00:05:52] Maya (AE): Yes we support offline license activation via an entitlement token exchange. You generate a CSR from the enclave HSM, provide it to Redwood via a secure channel (or on physical media), Redwood returns a signed entitlement blob which you then install locally. The runtime verifies the entitlement against the HSM. No phone-home required.

[00:06:11] Ellen (Security): How about cryptographic algorithms? We mandate FIPS 140-2 modules for any crypto operations used in signing or TLS. Can your runtime be compiled against FIPS libraries?

[00:06:23] Diego (SE): We have a FIPS-compatible build option and can integrate with customer-provided crypto libraries; this is something we'd validate during the POC. There may be additional packaging to produce the FIPS artifacts.

[00:06:38] Rajiv (ML): For model updates — how do you validate output quality (regression detection) in an offline flow? In the cloud you can run eval suites; here we have to do it locally.

[00:06:49] Diego (SE): We recommend shipping a regression eval bundle with each model release — a small set of golden prompts and expected outputs or metrics. The deployment manifest can include an eval phase: run tests locally, generate a report signed into the audit log. If the report shows regression, the operator can abort the rollout.

[00:07:09] Sam (Infra): What about image provenance and supply chain? We have a vendor security questionnaire that asks about SBOMs, COSIGN, SLSA levels, etc.

[00:07:21] Maya (AE): We can produce SBOMs and we support cosign-based signatures and attestations up to SLSA attestation levels. We'll capture the expected fields in the checklist.

[00:07:33] Kenji (DevOps): Will we need a local container registry? We have Nexus but it's not accessible from outside.

[00:07:41] Diego (SE): Yes an internal registry or artifact store is required for convenience. We can push tarballs or OCI images to your registry. Alternatively, we can provide a simple local registry packaged with the deployment.

[00:07:53] Priya (CTO): Maintenance windows — our lab only allows quarterly windows for major updates and monthly security patches. How do you support staggered patching?

[00:08:04] Diego (SE): The manifest supports specifying maintenance windows and staged rollouts. For security patches we can create smaller patch bundles that only update the runtime, and you can schedule them in your monthly windows. Major model rollouts can be scheduled for your quarterly window.

[00:08:18] Ellen (Security): Do you have a whitepaper on offline attestation and the entitlements flow? I looked briefly on the site but need something specific.

[00:08:26] Maya (AE): Yes — we'll send the private deployment whitepaper and a specific air-gap / offline attestation appendix.

[00:08:33] Priya (CTO): Pricing — high level thoughts? We are trying to decide between Dedicated in our secure colo vs Private fully isolated.

[00:08:43] Maya (AE): Dedicated is hosted in Redwood-managed colo with dedicated pools; it's easier for YC-type startups but not suitable if you require physical isolation. Private (on-prem) is a license plus support and entitlements; cost includes an initial deployment fee, annual license, and optional extended support. We'll send a comparative pricing matrix with TCO guidance for GPU vs CPU-only.

[00:09:02] Rajiv (ML): Any constraints on models we can bring? We want to use an OSS model family and fine-tune with our proprietary data. Is fine-tuning supported offline?

[00:09:13] Diego (SE): Fine-tuning in an entirely air-gapped environment is possible but heavier; you'd need to transfer training artifacts and snapshot registries. For this engagement our focus is serving inference; fine-tune pipelines are a more involved project but we can scope it in the POC if needed.

[00:09:29] Sam (Infra): On storage — how much disk per model? We need to budget NVMe vs HDD.

[00:09:36] Diego (SE): Rough numbers: a quantized 13B might be ~25-35GB depending on format and sharding. The runtime needs space for model shards, KV cache (if you enable large context), and local logs. We will provide a sizing doc with exact numbers per model variant.

[00:09:51] Kenji (DevOps): Backups — do you recommend snapshots to offline media? We prefer offline immutable backups for both model binaries and logs.

[00:09:59] Diego (SE): Yes, snapshots to encrypted archival media is standard. We can provide recommended retention and rotation procedures.

[00:10:08] Priya (CTO): Timeframes — if we want a POC, when can Redwood start?

[00:10:15] Maya (AE): We can start the POC once we align on hardware and NDA. Typical timeline: 2 weeks prep (artifact packaging and bench config), 1 week for on-site/remote benchmark, then a 2–3 week evaluation period. So earliest start would be end of March if we move quickly.

[00:10:31] Ellen (Security): Are there any dependencies on cloud vendor keys or services? We need to avoid any cloud KMS that requires external calls.

[00:10:40] Diego (SE): No dependencies — we can integrate with your on-prem HSM. The offline activation uses signed blobs and hardware-bound keys.

[00:10:50] Priya (CTO): One more question — support model during POC: if we hit a bug, how do we triage without backchannel?

[00:10:58] Maya (AE): We provide a war room cadence where you can push debug bundles — logs and traces — to a secured transfer node. Optionally, we can co-locate an engineer onsite or provide step-by-step reproduction guidance so you can collect the artifacts and ship them securely to Redwood's secure intake for urgent fixes.

[00:11:17] Rajiv (ML): For evaluation of quality regressions we want a harness that runs automatically on the enclave — the offline eval bundle you mentioned. Can you provide the harness code?

[00:11:26] Diego (SE): Yes we will provide an eval harness that runs locally and produces a signed report; it's a small container that you include in the bundle.

[00:11:36] Priya (CTO): Any gotchas we should be aware of?

[00:11:40] Diego (SE): A few: 1) artifact signing and key management needs strict process definition early, 2) initial bootstrapping often requires careful alignment of clocks and certificates in the enclave, and 3) if you choose CPU-only, make sure to validate tail latency during the bench — sometimes the p95 is worse than expected for chatty prompts.

[00:12:00] Sam (Infra): Regarding clocks — we can't sync to public NTP. We do have an internal time authority. Will that work?

[00:12:07] Diego (SE): Yes, an internal time source is fine; we just need consistent clocks for signed logs and certificate validity checks.

[00:12:15] Maya (AE): I want to recap and make sure we have agreement on next steps — Diego, you'll draft the air-gap deployment checklist and the signed image process; I'll send pricing and the whitepaper; Priya, you'll share anonymized request logs and p95 targets; we schedule bench week the week of 2026-03-22. Any objections?

[00:12:35] Priya (CTO): No objections, that works.

[00:12:39] Ellen (Security): Please include the FIPS build notes and SBOM examples in the checklist.

[00:12:44] Diego (SE): Will do.

[00:12:48] Maya (AE): Great. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and a calendar invite for the bench.

[00:12:55] Priya (CTO): Thank you.

[00:12:58] -- call ends approximately 55 minutes later --

Notes about transcription: Occasional overlaps, some product names misheard (e.g., "A5000" transcribed as "A five thousand"), standard Fireflies-style punctuation and filler words preserved.

Referenced artifacts/links: "private-deployment-whitepaper.pdf" (to be shared), "offline-deploy-checklist.xlsx" (to be authored), HW sizing spreadsheet (Redwood to send)
